title: Week 3 — instructor solutions
text:
Reusable template and scenarios

Watch me: build an Excel template






SolutionSolution 7 






Put sample inputs in labelled cells: estimate, sample size, confidence level, and either \(s\) for a mean or success count for a proportion. For an unknown-\(\sigma\) mean, use =T.INV.2T(1-confidence,n-1) and =s/SQRT(n). For a proportion, use =NORM.S.INV((1+confidence)/2) and =SQRT(phat*(1-phat)/n). Margin is critical value times standard error; bounds are estimate minus/plus margin. Check random sampling and, for the simple proportion interval, sufficiently many successes and failures.






Now you try: scenario analysis






SolutionSolution 8 






At fixed estimate and sample size, 90% gives the narrowest interval, then 95%, then 99%. At fixed variability, increasing \(n\) from 50 to 200 to 800 halves the standard error each time. For a mean, \(SE=s/\sqrt n\) (or \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) when known); for a proportion, \(SE=\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\). A manager can plan for wider intervals at higher confidence and can quadruple a random sample to roughly halve margin of error; neither tactic repairs biased sampling.

title: Week 3 — instructor solutions
text:
Retrieval and closing checks
A parameter describes the population; a statistic is calculated from a sample. In \(P(A\mid B)\), the denominator is the number or probability in group \(B\). A \(t\) distribution accounts for uncertainty from estimating the population SD in mean inference. Large datasets can still miss part of the target population. Sampling variation shrinks as \(n\) grows; selection bias does not. The law of large numbers says averages stabilise toward a population mean under appropriate sampling, while the central limit theorem supports an approximately Normal sampling distribution of the mean under suitable conditions as \(n\) grows. Report interval bounds as evidence with assumptions, not certainty about a fixed parameter.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Proportions: notation
Source: ETF1100 Week 7 seminar, page 6
A proportion is the relative frequency of a characteristic, so it lies between 0 and 1.

Population proportion: \pi.
Sample proportion: \hat p=X/n, where X observations have the characteristic among n observations.

Grocery-store example: 47 of 80 shoppers used a trolley, so \hat p=47/80=0.5875. The others used a basket (28) or carried items by hand (5).

title: Business Statistics
section: Proportions and confidence intervals in practice
text:
Proportions and confidence intervals in practice
Source: ETF1100 Week 7 seminar, page 7
A study of adolescent smoking prevalence in Australia reports an estimated 13.2% prevalence of ever smoking in 2022–2023, with a 95% confidence interval of 12.7% to 13.6%. It compares this with a projected background trend of 5.8%, with a 95% interval of 5.6% to 6.0%.
The intervals express uncertainty around the estimates. Source example: Egger et al., Medical Journal of Australia (2025), DOI: 10.5694/mja2.70000.

title: Business Statistics
section: Sampling distribution of a sample proportion
text:
Sampling distribution of a sample proportion
Source: ETF1100 Week 7 seminar, page 8
We use the sample proportion \hat p to estimate the population proportion \pi. The value of \hat p changes from sample to sample.
\operatorname{SE}(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{n}}.
For a sufficiently large sample, \hat p is approximately normal with mean \pi and this standard error. The source checks n\pi\geq5 and n(1-\pi)\geq5.

title: Business Statistics
section: Which proportion goes into the standard error?
text:
Which proportion goes into the standard error?
Source: ETF1100 Week 7 seminar, page 9
For a hypothesis test, use the null benchmark \pi_0:
\operatorname{SE}_0(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{\pi_0(1-\pi_0)}{n}},\qquad n\pi_0\geq5,\quad n(1-\pi_0)\geq5.
For a confidence interval, \pi is unknown, so estimate the standard error with \hat p:
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}},\qquad n\hat p\geq5,\quad n(1-\hat p)\geq5.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Why use a confidence interval?
Source: ETF1100 Week 7 seminar, page 10
One sample gives one point estimate, \hat p, for the unknown population proportion \pi.
Because samples vary, \hat p will not always equal \pi. A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for \pi rather than only the single estimate.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Confidence interval for a proportion
Source: ETF1100 Week 7 seminar, page 11
The confidence level is 1-\alpha. For example, a 95% confidence level has \alpha=0.05; a 90% confidence level has \alpha=0.10.
When n\hat p\geq5 and n(1-\hat p)\geq5, the approximate interval is
\hat p\;\pm\;z^*\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}},\qquad z^*=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2).
In Excel: =NORM.S.INV(1-alpha/2). At 95% confidence, z^*\approx1.96.

Hypothesis Testing - Classic Example
An hypothesis test is conducted to decide between two hypotheses: the null H0 and the alternative, H1. H0: Defendant is not guilty (‘status quo’; default) H1: Defendant is guilty (experimental/research hypothesis) Reject H0: GUILTY! There IS enough evidence against H0 - the defendant is guilty. Do not reject H0: NOT GUILTY (INNOCENT!) There IS NOT enough evidence against H0 - the defendant is not guilty. 5

title: Business Statistics
text:
Source: Workshop5_Hypothesis_Testing_II.pdf, page 9
Mechanics of Hypothesis Testing: p-value
Judging whether or not the test statistic is outstandingly “far from zero” in the direction of the alternative. It is the probability of getting the test statistic assuming that H0 is true. p-value = P(Test statistic |H0 is true) If the p-value is small, then the test statistic is far from zero. (In the direction of the alternative hypothesis.) A smaller p-value means that there is stronger evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis. 9

Visual from source page 9.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Source: Workshop5_Hypothesis_Testing_II.pdf, page 10
Interpreting the p-value
P-value should be interpreted as the level of “evidence” in favour of the null hypothesis, when compared against the ALTERNATIVE hypothesis. A small p-value: Indicates little evidence in support of the H0; we have reason to reject H0 in favour of H1 A large p-value: Indicates considerable evidence in support of the H0; we do not have reason to reject H0 in favour of H1. Advantage: An advantage of p-values is that we can perform hypothesis tests at all significance levels without finding a new critical value. 10

Errors in Hypothesis Testing

Type I Error is directly related to the significance level: 
Pr(Type I Error) = \alpha{}

title: Business Statistics
text:
Source: Workshop5_Hypothesis_Testing_II.pdf, page 24
Type I and II errors
Since the conclusions that we draw are based on sample data - using a decision rule, there is the chance of making two possible errors: Type I Error: Reject H0 when it’s actually true. Conclude guilty, when defendant is innocent. - The probability of a Type I error is denoted by \alpha. - This value is also referred to as the “Level of Significance”. Type II Error: Do not reject H0 when it’s actually false. Conclude not guilty, when defendant is guilty. - The probability of making a Type II error is denoted by \beta. - (1- \beta) is referred to as the “Power of the Test”. NOTE: If we retain the null, we do not say it is true. We do not say we “accept” it; we simply do not reject it. 24

title: Business Statistics
text:
Source: Workshop5_Hypothesis_Testing_II.pdf, page 25
Type I and II errors
The smaller we make \alpha, the bigger \beta becomes. This inverse relationship must be considered when choosing the significance level \alpha. (1-\beta) is referred to as the “Power of the Test”. The true ‘state of the world’ Statistical Decision H0 TRUE H0 FALSE Type II error Do not reject H0 Correct decision 
Pr(Type II error) = \beta{}
 Type I error Reject H0 Correct decision 
Pr(Type 1 error) = \alpha{}

Watch me: categorical relationship / Now you try: explain the association






SolutionSolution 3 






The outcome is high satisfaction and the groups are app users and non-users. The given rates, 72% and 61%, are conditional because each uses its own group as denominator. The observed gap is 11 percentage points. Plausible confounders include age, prior satisfaction, loyalty or spending. A defensible sentence is: “High satisfaction was 11 percentage points more common among sampled app users; this observational comparison does not establish that using the app increased satisfaction.” A contingency table with group counts would show precision and support further analysis.

For IncomeSpend, put Income on X and Spend on Y. =CORREL(B2:B806,C2:C806) gives 0.7421, a moderately strong positive linear association. Income ranges from AUD 15,006 to 99,960. The scatterplot should be checked for departures from a straight-line trend and unusual residuals before describing prediction quality.
For HouseSize, plot market price (AUD thousands) against house age. =CORREL(C2:C24,A2:A24) gives −0.5766 (since \(R^2=0.3325\) and the fitted slope is negative). The plot supports a negative linear summary, though the 23 properties show substantial spread. Check the scatterplot before assuming linearity.

SolutionSolution 5 







\(r=0\) only rules out a linear sample association; a curved relationship may remain. (2) Correlation alone does not identify causation. (3) Correlation is unit-free, so “0.8 kilograms” is incorrect. (4) An unusual store must be checked for data error or a substantive reason, and any exclusion disclosed; deleting it to improve \(r\) biases the report.

Simple regression

Watch me: regression in Excel / Now you try: interpret IncomeSpend






SolutionSolution 6 






In Data > Data Analysis > Regression, set Spend as Y and Income as X, select Labels and residual output. The fitted equation is \(\widehat{Spend}=\mathbf{8254.58+0.295615\,Income}\), both money variables in AUD. At zero income the line predicts AUD 8,254.58, but zero is outside the observed income range and the intercept should not be used as a practical forecast. For an AUD 1 income increase, predicted mean spend increases by about AUD 0.296, conditional on this simple model; for AUD 10,000, by AUD 2,956.15. The positive slope matches the positive correlation. \(R^2=\mathbf{0.5508}\) and the two-sided slope p-value is about \(1.11\times10^{-141}\).






Watch me: predict from the line / Now you try: HouseSize regression






SolutionSolution 7 






The demonstration equation \(8254.575+0.296\,Income\) is rounded; for an in-range income of AUD 60,000 it predicts about AUD 26,015. This is a fitted mean, not a promise about an individual’s spend. Using the unrounded fitted slope gives about AUD 25,991.5; the difference illustrates why coefficient precision matters.
For age, the fitted line is \(\widehat{Price}_{000}=\mathbf{1088.03-10.8883\,Age}\), with price in AUD thousands. Each additional year is associated with AUD 10,888 lower predicted price on average; five years correspond to AUD 54,441 lower. \(R^2=\mathbf{0.3325}\), so age explains about 33.25% of sample price variation under this line. The slope p-value is 0.00397, supporting a population linear association subject to assumptions. For the first house (age 35, observed AUD 630,000), fitted price is AUD 706,944, residual −AUD 76,944.

IncomeSpend residuals range roughly −AUD 18,494 to +AUD 15,685; a strength is its clear positive relationship, while a limitation is considerable individual scatter and omitted factors such as household size. title: Week 5 — instructor solutions
text:
Retrieval and closing checks
For two categorical variables, compare conditional percentages in a contingency table. Independence means the outcome probability does not change with the grouping event in the population. A small p-value measures incompatibility with a null model under assumptions; it does not establish cause or importance. Scatterplots require two numerical variables, with X as explanatory and Y as response. For regression, report units, equation, \(R^2\), slope evidence, an in-range prediction, a residual and a limitation, as the worked examples above do.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Recap: simple linear regression
\widehat Y_i=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1X_i.

The intercept predicts Y at X=0; that may be outside the useful range.
The slope is the change in predicted Y for a one-unit rise in X.
A positive slope indicates an upward association; a negative slope indicates a downward association.

Source: ETF1100 Week 9 seminar, page 5.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Recap: multiple linear regression
\widehat Y_i=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1X_{1i}+\cdots+\widehat\beta_kX_{ki}.
The intercept predicts Y when every predictor is zero, which may not describe a meaningful case.
Each slope compares observations that differ by one unit in that predictor while the other included predictors are held fixed.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 seminar, page 6.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Steps in a coefficient test

State the null and alternative hypotheses.
Calculate the test statistic.
Obtain the p-value from Excel output.
Reject H_0 when p<\alpha; otherwise fail to reject it.
Explain the conclusion in the business context and in terms of the alternative claim.

Source: ETF1100 Week 9 seminar, page 8.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Hypotheses for one slope
For predictor X_k, test H_0:\beta_k=0 against one of:

H_1:\beta_k>0 for a positive conditional relationship;
H_1:\beta_k<0 for a negative conditional relationship; or
H_1:\beta_k\ne0 for any conditional linear relationship.

Choose the alternative from the question before inspecting the estimate.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 seminar, page 9.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Slope test statistic
t=\frac{\widehat\beta_k-0}{SE(\widehat\beta_k)},\qquad df=n-k-1,
where k is the number of predictors and the extra 1 counts the intercept. Excel’s regression output reports the estimate, standard error and t statistic.
For Beds in the full real-estate model, t=47.426/22.866\approx2.074 with df=324.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 seminar, page 10.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Read the p-value
The P-value column in Excel’s Regression output is for a two-sided slope test.

For H_1:\beta_k\ne0, use the displayed value.
For a one-sided alternative in the direction of the estimate, divide it by two.
If the estimate points opposite to the one-sided alternative, do not use a small halved value as evidence for that claim.

For Beds, Excel reports two-sided p=0.03886.

title: Business Statistics
text:
One-sided example: bedrooms
Claim: more bedrooms are associated with a higher property price, holding the other predictors fixed.
H_0:\beta_{Beds}=0,\qquad H_1:\beta_{Beds}>0.
The estimate is positive (47.426) and Excel’s two-sided p is 0.03886, so the one-sided p\approx0.01943. At \alpha=0.05, reject H_0.
There is evidence of a positive conditional association with price. This observational model does not establish causation.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 seminar, page 13.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Two-sided example: car spaces
Claim: car spaces have some conditional association with property price.
H_0:\beta_{Cars}=0,\qquad H_1:\beta_{Cars}\ne0.
Excel reports \widehat\beta_{Cars}=14.544 and two-sided p=0.5235. At \alpha=0.05, fail to reject H_0.
The data do not provide strong evidence of an additional linear contribution from Cars in this specification.

For a two-sided coefficient test, a small p-value supports retaining a predictor. A large p-value invites a comparison with a model that omits it.
Here, Cars has p=0.5235. The source refits a model without Cars. Compare fit, changes in other slopes and business meaning before choosing the reduced model.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Compare and evaluate models
The source compares candidate models using:

R^2, the share of observed outcome variation explained in sample; and
residual diagnostics, which reveal patterns or changing spread left unexplained by the model.

Also compare adjusted R^2 and the business purpose when deciding between specifications.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 seminar, page 17.

title: Business Statistics
text:
What R^2 means
Write each observed value as fitted value plus residual:
Y_i=\widehat Y_i+e_i.
R^2 measures the proportion of total sample variation in Y explained by the fitted model. It lies between 0 and 1. Values near 1 mean a larger share is explained in the sample; they do not prove the model is useful for every prediction.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 seminar, page 18.

title: Business Statistics
text:
The sum-of-squares decomposition
SST=\sum_i(Y_i-\bar Y)^2,\quad SSR=\sum_i(\widehat Y_i-\bar Y)^2,\quad SSE=\sum_i(Y_i-\widehat Y_i)^2.
For least-squares regression with an intercept, SST=SSR+SSE.

SST: total variation around the sample mean.
SSR: variation explained by the regression.
SSE: variation left in the residuals.

R^2=\frac{SSR}{SST}.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 seminar, page 19.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Fit as explained variation
The source’s diagram restates the relationship
SST=SSR+SSE,\qquad R^2=\frac{SSR}{SST}=1-\frac{SSE}{SST}.
A model with a larger explained share has a larger in-sample R^2. Adding predictors can also raise R^2 without improving usefulness, so compare model complexity and residual behaviour.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 seminar, page 20.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Real-estate R^2 example
For the reduced Beds + Baths + Area model, R^2\approx0.604.
About 60% of the observed variation in property price is explained by this predictor set; about 40% remains unexplained by the model.
Adjusted R^2\approx0.600 accounts for predictor count and sample size. The source focuses mainly on R^2.

Real-estate residual plot

The residuals are roughly centred on zero, but their spread is larger for properties with greater area. Forecast uncertainty may therefore vary with property size.

Do not enter categories as arbitrary numbers such as Water =1, Tea =2, Coffee =3: that would impose a numerical spacing that has no business meaning.
Instead, represent a category with a dummy variable taking 0 or 1.

Interpret a dummy coefficient
For a dummy D_k, \widehat\beta_k is the predicted difference between D_k=1 and the base category holding the other predictors fixed.

Positive coefficient: predicted outcome is higher than the base.
Negative coefficient: predicted outcome is lower than the base.

The intercept refers to the base category when other numerical predictors are zero.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Overall F-test
The overall test asks whether the predictor set has any linear relationship with Y:
H_0:\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_k=0,\qquad H_1:\text{at least one slope is nonzero}.
F=\frac{SSR/k}{SSE/(n-k-1)}.
Excel reports the F statistic and Significance F in the ANOVA block. Reject H_0 when its p-value is below \alpha.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 seminar, page 31.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Simple linear regression model
The population model relates a numerical outcome Y_i to one input X_i:
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i.
\beta_0 and \beta_1 are population parameters. The error \varepsilon_i captures the part of Y_i not described by the line.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 tutorial solutions, page 3.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Fitted line and residual
Estimate the population coefficients from sample data:
\widehat Y_i=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1X_i,\qquad e_i=Y_i-\widehat Y_i.
The fitted value predicts an observation using the estimated line. The residual is observed minus fitted value, in the units of Y.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 tutorial solutions, page 4.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Least squares
Choose the fitted coefficients to minimise the sum of squared residuals:
SSE=\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_i^2=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\widehat Y_i)^2.
Squaring prevents positive and negative residuals from cancelling and penalises large misses more heavily.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 tutorial solutions, page 5.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Interpret simple-regression coefficients
In \widehat Y_i=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1X_i:

\widehat\beta_0 predicts Y when X=0; it may lack practical meaning if zero is outside the observed range.
\widehat\beta_1 is the predicted change in Y for a one-unit increase in X.

A positive slope rises with X; a negative slope falls with X.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 tutorial solutions, page 6.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Why simple slopes can mislead
In real estate, Area, Beds, Baths and Cars can move together. A simple regression of Price on Area can attribute to Area variation also associated with the omitted property features.
Omitting a relevant predictor may bias a slope estimate. Multiple regression lets us compare properties at fixed values of the other included features, although it does not by itself prove causation.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 tutorial solutions, page 7.

title: Business Statistics
text:
Interpret multiple-regression slopes
\widehat Y_i=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1X_{1i}+\widehat\beta_2X_{2i}+\cdots+\widehat\beta_kX_{ki}.
\widehat\beta_k is the predicted change in Y for one more unit of X_k, holding the other included predictors fixed.
The intercept refers to all predictors equal to zero and may not represent a realistic case.
Source: ETF1100 Week 9 tutorial solutions, page 8.

title: Archived Week 7 business-modelling solutions
text:
Pilot and demand model

Watch me: inspect the pilot / Now you try: data and decision audit






SolutionSolution 1 






The observational unit is a comparable store-week; there are 24 rows. Price is X (AUD), units sold Y (whole units). Observed prices are AUD 50–105, with two observations at each listed price. The scatterplot is strongly downward and approximately linear, with modest spread around the line. Check all rows for missing or misplaced values. A line is useful for summarising demand over the tested range, but future demand can differ because of season, promotion, competitors or imperfect comparability. The pilot does not supply unit cost, fixed cost or weekly production capacity; those come from business assumptions.






Watch me: run Regression / Now you try: explain the regression






SolutionSolution 2 






Using Units_sold as Y and Price_AUD as X, ToolPak gives
\[\widehat{Units}=\mathbf{701.033800-5.011189\,Price_{AUD}}.\]
Within the studied range, a one-AUD higher price is associated with about 5.01 fewer predicted units per comparable store-week. At AUD 80, predicted units are 300.139. \(R^2=\mathbf{0.99467}\); the slope p-value is extremely small. A strong pilot fit does not ensure that future store-week demand will follow the same relationship. Avoid predictions beyond AUD 50–105 without new evidence.






Watch me: validate before using coefficients / Now you try: output quality check






SolutionSolution 3 






For the first two pilot rows (both price AUD 50), fitted units are 450.474. Observed units are 442 and 457, so residuals are −8.474 and +6.526. The full pilot residuals range about −9.14 to +9.64 units. Confirm ToolPak output uses the correct Y/X roles, compare these rows with its residual output, inspect residual-versus-price for structure, and retain coefficient precision. The current listed-price predictions are positive.

title: Archived Week 7 business-modelling solutions
text:
Spreadsheet decision model

Watch me: connect output to inputs / Now you try: label and audit the model






SolutionSolution 4 






Paste 701.033800 to B7 and −5.011189 to B8 on Decision model (use more displayed ToolPak digits if available). B4 AUD 40 unit variable cost, B5 AUD 1,200 fixed weekly cost, and B6 340 units capacity are business assumptions, not regression estimates. In B13 enter =$B$7+$B$8*A13 and fill through row 24. At AUD 50 the prediction is 450.474, and at AUD 105 it is 174.859. Both are within the pilot range. A price beyond AUD 105 would extrapolate the line.






Watch me: apply the capacity rule / Watch me: calculate profit / Now you try: complete the scenario model






SolutionSolution 5 






Use =MAX(0,MIN(ROUNDDOWN(B13,0),$B$6)) in C13. Then D13 =A13*C13, E13 =$B$5+$B$4*C13, F13 =D13-E13; fill down. An audit formula in G13 can be =IF(B13<0,"Negative prediction",IF(ROUNDDOWN(B13,0)>$B$6,"Capacity binds","OK")). The first row has predicted demand 450.474, planned units 340, revenue AUD 17,000, cost AUD 14,800, profit AUD 2,200. The independent profit check is \((50-40)\times340-1200=2200\). =ROUND(B13,0) is valid Excel but violates the stated round-down rule; using uncapped predicted units in revenue also violates capacity.

SolutionSolution 6

title: Archived Week 7 business-modelling solutions
text:
Sensitivity and managerial brief

Watch me: stress-test one assumption / Now you try: two stress tests






SolutionSolution 7 






Restore baseline before each change. Raising unit cost to AUD 50 leaves capacity at 340 and changes the best listed price to AUD 95: 224 units and AUD 8,880 predicted profit. Setting capacity to 200 while restoring unit cost to AUD 40 changes the best listed price to AUD 100: 199 units and AUD 10,740 profit. Relative to baseline, the profit falls by AUD 2,420 in the cost case and AUD 560 in the capacity case; the cost increase has the larger profit impact, while the capacity reduction moves the chosen listed price farther. Do not change both inputs simultaneously when reporting these separate tests.






Group brief: recommend a launch price / Now you try: team working time






SolutionSolution 8 






A model brief could read: “The 24 store-week pilot yields \(\widehat{Units}=701.034-5.01119\,Price\), with \(R^2=0.9947\) and the AUD 50 residual check of −8.47 units. We use whole units rounded down, cap sales at 340, and calculate profit as \((Price-40)\times Units-1200\). Of the twelve listed prices, AUD 90 gives the largest baseline predicted profit, AUD 11,300; AUD 85 gives AUD 11,175. With unit cost AUD 50, AUD 95 is best at AUD 8,880; with capacity 200 and baseline cost, AUD 100 is best at AUD 10,740. Trial AUD 90 subject to monitoring actual units, costs and competitor response, and revisit if demand or capacity differs materially.” Include the completed formula table or a clearly labelled extract.






Watch me: critique a decision memo / Now you try: improve the memo






SolutionSolution 9 






Check one row independently using \((Price-UnitCost)\times PlannedUnits-FixedCost\), verify the recommendation is a listed price, and qualify “expected” or “predicted” profit rather than promising realised profit. State the whole-unit and capacity rules and compare each sensitivity with the same baseline. A useful revision adds a monitoring trigger, such as revisiting the price if actual weekly units at AUD 90 are consistently far from the 250 forecast. The pilot does not establish a causal price effect across all future conditions or a global optimum.

title: Archived Week 7 business-modelling solutions
text:
Retrieval and closing checks
Units sold is the demand-regression outcome; price is the predictor. The intercept is predicted units at zero price, outside this pilot’s range and not a useful decision forecast. The price slope is predicted units change per AUD 1 within the model. A fitted value is the model’s estimate of mean units; actual sales also include residual variation. Staying within AUD 50–105 avoids extrapolation. The decision’s inputs are costs, capacity and ToolPak coefficients; its objective is predicted profit; its rules are whole units, non-negative sales and capacity. The best listed baseline option is AUD 90, subject to the assumptions and monitoring conditions above.

title: Current weekly teaching content
text:
This summary reflects the material currently in weekN/slides.qmd, including worked examples and solutions. It describes the slide decks themselves; the revised schedule labels are maintained separately in course_info.R.



Week
Topics covered in the current slides




Week 1
Descriptive statistics; data types and variables; an Excel primer on cell references, formulas, copying formulas and summary functions; populations and samples; measures of centre and spread, including variance, standard deviation and coefficient of variation; distribution shape; histograms and box plots; Excel Analysis ToolPak and visualisation exercises using real estate data.


Week 2
Probability rules, unions, conditional probability, mutually exclusive and independent events; frequency and relative-frequency tables; joint probabilities and PivotTables; applied categorical-data examples; probability as area under a density; normal and standard normal distributions, including Excel calculations.


Week 3
Sampling distributions and the Central Limit Theorem; sampling variability and standard errors; normal-distribution applications; confidence-interval estimation for means and proportions, including z and t intervals; applied retail, graduate-income, account-balance and survey examples.


Week 4
Sample proportions, their sampling distributions and standard errors, confidence intervals for proportions and an applied prevalence example; evidence-based hypothesis tests for population means and proportions; null and alternative hypotheses; test statistics and p-values; significance levels and decisions; marketing, transaction-success and business-process examples; Type I and Type II errors and test power.


Week 5
Chi-square test of independence for categorical variables, including expected counts and worked examples; scatterplots, covariance and correlation for numerical variables, with Excel formulas and cautions about nonlinear patterns and causation; simple linear regression in Excel, coefficient interpretation, prediction, slope confidence intervals, R^2 and slope tests using real-estate and marketing examples.


Week 6
Multiple regression and model evaluation using the ETF1100 Week 9 seminar and tutorial solutions: conditional slope interpretation, coefficient tests and model reduction, R^2 and residual diagnostics, dummy variables for categorical predictors, the overall F-test, and an Excel travel-time regression exercise with worked answers. The real-estate and travel-time source workbooks are linked from the Week 6 page.


Week 7
Introduction to time series; line charts of observed and deseasonalised values; time indexing and linear trend forecasts with Excel INTERCEPT and SLOPE; supplied seasonal indices and multiplicative forecasts; fitting on earlier training data, comparing forecasts with observed values in a later historical test period, then evaluating absolute errors with Excel ABS and mean absolute deviation (MAD). Worked examples use chocolate-bar and retail-sales data.


Week 8
Revision and examination practice; exam format and authorised materials; worked questions and solutions covering the unit’s statistical topics; closing reminders and source-page SETU material.
